article.overview: A plasma analyser measures the charged particles, mainly electrons and ions, that make up plasma in space. It characterises them by energy and, in many designs, by arrival direction and sometimes by mass. The Moon has no global magnetic field and only a very thin exosphere, so the solar wind reaches the lunar surface and the lunar environment is shaped directly by it; a plasma analyser records the state of that local plasma. Two flown examples are documented here. The Apollo 12 Solar Wind Spectrometer (SWS) operated on the lunar surface as part of the Apollo 12 Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP), with data from 19 November 1969 to 25 March 1976 [2]. The Plasma Energy Angle and Composition Experiment (PACE) flew on Japan's SELENE (Kaguya) lunar orbiter, a different vantage point, so the two instruments' specifications must not be combined [6][7].
article.description: A plasma analyser uses a sensor that responds to charged particles and sorts them by energy. Two families are used in the examples here. A Faraday cup collects the charge carried by incoming particles on a collector, and grids in front of it set which energies are admitted; the Apollo 12 SWS used seven such cups, each with five grids and a collector [4]. An electrostatic analyser uses electric fields to select particles by energy and direction; the PACE sensors are named ESA-S1, ESA-S2 (electron analysers), IMA (ion mass analyser) and IEA (ion energy analyser) [6]. The term 'plasma analyser' is used in this catalogue for a general class. Related catalogue entries are separate payload classes and are not described here: 117 Solar wind analyser, 119 Langmuir probe, 120 Ion spectrometer, 121 Electron spectrometer, 122 Energetic neutral atom analyser, and 125 Plasma wave instrument.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The main purpose of a lunar plasma analyser is to measure the solar wind and the plasma environment near the Moon, including how that plasma changes with time and how it interacts with the surface. Its measurements are expressed as particle flux against energy, and as flow parameters derived from those fluxes. The Apollo 12 SWS archive is organised as time-ordered plasma parameter tables at 28-second and 1-hour resolution [2][3].

Applications reported for the Apollo SWS in secondary summaries include comparison of solar-wind plasma at the lunar surface with spacecraft measurements far from the Moon, observations during lunar night, and observations at lunar sunrise, when the spectra were reported to be highly variable [9]. These qualitative findings were not checked against primary papers in this run. The JAXA page describes PACE as measuring low-energy electrons and ions, with electron sensors covering energies below 15 keV and ion sensors below 28 keV/q [6].
article.operating_principle:
A Faraday cup collects charged particles that enter its opening onto a collector, producing a current proportional to the particle flux in the energy range the grids admit. The Apollo 12 SWS cups were modulated: five grids applied an AC modulating field to incoming particles, which also shielded the sensitive preamplifiers [4]. The instrument covered electrons from 6 to 1330 eV in 7 energy steps spaced by a factor of 2, and positive ions from 18 to 9780 eV in 14 steps spaced by a factor of the square root of 2 [4][5]. Seven cups were arranged so that they viewed slightly overlapping parts of the lunar sky: cup 7 pointed near vertically and cups 1 to 6 faced 60 degrees from vertical [3][4]. The archive reports one measurement sequence every 28.1 seconds [4][2].

For PACE, the JAXA description states that electron and ion sensors measure low-energy particles with angular resolutions given per sensor and a 1-second sampling interval [6]. The internal energy-selection design of the electrostatic analysers was not read in the pages accessed, so the general principle above is not a verified description of PACE hardware [6][7].
article.scientific_importance: Direct plasma measurements at the lunar surface are rare. The 1970 NASA/JPL report on the Apollo 12 solar-wind spectrometer and particle energy spectra at the lunar surface records the scientific intent of the instrument [1]. Plasma measurements on the surface and in orbit are needed to understand how the solar wind reaches a body without a global magnetic field, and how it interacts with the surface [1][9]. Orbital measurements, such as the PACE instrument on SELENE, extend these observations across the lunar environment [6][7]. The catalogue documents a broad class, so the scientific value of any single new analyser depends on its energy range, angular coverage and time resolution compared with the existing instruments.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a plasma analyser. Sensor count, energy range, angular coverage, mass and power depend on the target plasma, the platform and the measurement goal. The two examples below are very different: a surface instrument with seven Faraday cups, and an orbiter sensor set with four heads. Values are attributed to a named instrument and source, and they are not directly comparable.

examples.sensor_configuration: Seven modulated Faraday cups opened toward different, but slightly overlapping, parts of the lunar sky; each cup has a circular opening, five grids and a collector [4].
examples.energy_steps: Electrons: 7 steps, factor of 2 apart. Positive ions: 14 steps, factor of the square root of 2 apart [4].
examples.flux_range_particles_cm2_s: 2.5E6 to 2.5E11 (as stated in the PDS description) [4]
examples.deployment: Part of the Apollo 12 ALSEP; placed 4 m south of the central station (3.00942 S, 23.42458 W); cup 4 faced east [3][4].
examples.operations: Background data taken with covers on; covers removed 20 November 1969 about 15:30 UT; standby from 3 March 1976 during lunar night; turned off 15 January 1977 [4]. Data tables run to 25 March 1976 [2].
examples.qualification: Mass, power and dimensions are instrument values from the PDS archive description [4]. They are not the mass of the whole ALSEP package.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The Apollo 12 SWS has deployed dimensions of 30.5 x 28.2 x 34.5 cm [4]. The PACE external dimensions were not found in the sources accessed, so no comparison of envelope is made.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The Apollo 12 SWS mass is given as 5.7 kg [4]. PACE mass is not given in the sources accessed. Mass figures for the surface ALSEP and for the orbiter payload are not comparable to the instrument-only mass above.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The Apollo 12 SWS drew 12.5 W in total, as stated in the PDS description [4]. The PACE power requirement was not found in the sources accessed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
On the lunar surface, a plasma analyser is exposed to vacuum, extreme temperature cycling and the lunar night. The Apollo 12 SWS was protected by dust covers over the cup entrances during extravehicular activity and lunar-module ascent [4]. Its covers were removed on 20 November 1969 at about 15:30 UT, after background data had been recorded with the covers in place [4]. The instrument drew 12.5 W in total and was placed in standby during the lunar night from 3 March 1976 to free power for the central station; it was turned off on 15 January 1977 to increase power for the central station's thermal control [4]. These notes show that the power and thermal budget shaped operations as well as the sensor design.

For an orbiter such as SELENE, the environment is vacuum and radiation-exposed, with the plasma population varying along the orbit. The orbit and thermal parameters of PACE were not verified in the pages accessed [6].
article.limitations: A single plasma analyser samples a limited part of the energy and angular space at any given time, so a single instrument cannot describe the whole plasma environment. A surface instrument samples one location; the Apollo 12 SWS was turned off after about seven years of operation [4]. Cup geometry and the viewing direction of each cup strongly affect what the instrument can measure, and the Apollo 12 cup orientation is documented only for that mission [3][4]. Published energy ranges for PACE differ depending on whether they are design values or in-flight values, and this could not be resolved in this run [6][7].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A surface plasma analyser is delivered as part of a lunar surface experiment package. An orbiting plasma analyser is delivered as one instrument set on a lunar orbiter. The two routes are different and are described separately below.
transportation_process: Surface (Apollo 12 SWS): integrate the instrument into the Apollo 12 ALSEP package on Earth; transport it to the Moon with the Apollo 12 mission; deploy it on the surface [4].
Surface (Apollo 12 SWS): the instrument was placed 4 metres south of the central station, with cup 4 facing east, and its as-deployed axes were within the stated specifications [3][4].
Surface: power and data for the SWS were provided within the ALSEP; the instrument's total power is 12.5 W [4].

Orbiter (PACE): integrate the sensor set on the SELENE spacecraft; transport to the Moon; achieve lunar orbit; commission and operate the sensors [6]. Launch-vehicle and orbit-insertion details were not verified in the pages accessed.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Apollo 12 SWS was set up on the surface as one component of the Apollo 12 ALSEP [4]. The archive describes placement 4 m south of the central station and an east-west axis set 2.8 degrees north of east and 2.5 degrees off level, with the west edge low; the archive states these were within the instrument specifications [4]. PACE is an orbital instrument of SELENE (Kaguya), so surface deployment does not apply [6].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 12 SWS was part of the Apollo 12 ALSEP, and its data span 19 November 1969 to 25 March 1976 [2]. PACE is a documented orbital example on SELENE (Kaguya) [6][7].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: The compatibility of a plasma analyser with a particular lander or orbiter would need to be assessed from its mass, dimensions, mounting, power, data interfaces and thermal requirements. No lander or spacecraft compatibility is asserted here, because verified interface evidence for a specific vehicle was not collected in this run.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 12 SWS made direct plasma measurements on the lunar surface and operated for about seven years [1][2][4]. The 1970 NASA/JPL report describes its particle energy spectra at the lunar surface [1]. Secondary summaries report further findings, including no detectable plasma in lunar-night shadow, highly variable spectra at lunar sunrise, distinction between interplanetary and magnetosheath plasma, and a shock from the Apollo 13 S-IVB impact observed in the Apollo 15 context [9]. These findings were not verified against primary papers in this run. PACE is documented in the SELENE mission literature as an orbital plasma experiment, and its in-flight results are described in the 2010 paper [7], which was not opened here.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name 'plasma analyser' describes a class of instruments rather than one standard design. The Apollo 12 SWS and PACE are not interchangeable: one is a surface instrument with seven Faraday cups and the other is an orbiter sensor set with four heads. Values such as mass, dimensions, power and energy range must always be tied to a named instrument and source. The following items remain unresolved in this run: the Apollo 12 SWS principal investigator is named only in a secondary summary; the PACE mass, power and dimensions are not given in the sources accessed; the PACE in-flight performance paper [7] could not be opened; and the NASA Apollo 12 Preliminary Science Report chapter on the SWS [8] could not be read.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Web search budget for the session was exhausted during this run; research relied on direct fetches of PDS archive, ARCNAV, NTRS and JAXA pages.
Only two verified images are included. No verified Apollo 12 SWS hardware photograph or PACE launch/orbit image was found; the transportation section has no images.
The Apollo 12 SWS energy ranges come from the ARCNAV context page and the PDS instrument description; they are consistent between those two sources.

PACE energy ranges and angular resolutions are from the JAXA project page, which is a design-stage description (copyright 2007). The 2010 in-flight paper [7] was not opened; a search summary reported different in-flight energy ranges that could not be verified.
The Apollo 12 SWS principal investigator, and the qualitative findings in the Historical Significance section, come only from a secondary summary (Wikipedia) and are flagged as unverified.
The Apollo 12 Preliminary Science Report chapter (a12_psr_ch5_sws.pdf) could not be read in this run.
PACE mass, power and dimensions were not found in the accessed sources; they are null, not estimated.
The PDS-hosted cup-configuration image and the JAXA PACE figure were retrieved and checked visually; rights and reuse terms for both were not verified.
